titulo: Atividade antimicrobiana da nanocelulose bacteriana contendo Caesalpinia ferrea
titulo_curto: Jucá inside nanocellulose: a natural dressing against bacteria

em_1_minuto.titulo: A plant used to heal wounds
em_1_minuto.texto: Jucá (Caesalpinia ferrea), a Brazilian tree also known as Brazilian ironwood (pau-ferro), is used in folk medicine to heal wounds and relieve inflammation and pain.
They loaded jucá bark extract into nanocellulose membranes made by bacteria and tested whether they released the extract and blocked bacteria.
The membrane released the extract for up to 40 hours, peaking at 30 hours, and every sample stopped the growth of the three bacteria tested.
Combining the qualities of nanocellulose with those of jucá could lead to a dressing. The next step is to test whether it helps healing.

average bacteria-free zone against E. coli and P. aeruginosa
peak extract release: 218 µg/mL of protein

secoes.lede: A tree from Brazilian folk medicine and a material produced by bacteria, together in a possible dressing.

blocos.html:
In Brazil, Caesalpinia ferrea (also called Libidibia ferrea) is known as pau-ferro, jucá, ibirá-obi or muirá-obi. It grows throughout the country, mainly in the North and Northeast, such as in Pernambuco and Ceará. Leaves, fruits, pods and bark are used in teas, syrups, extracts and macerates.

Studies have already found flavonoids, saponins, coumarins, phenols and tannins in the plant, especially gallic acid and ellagic acid. Because of them, jucá has healing, antimicrobial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant action.

Bacterial nanocellulose is a very pure cellulose made of nanofibers, produced by bacteria. It holds about 99% water, contains no animal-derived components and is already used as a temporary skin substitute and as a dressing for burns and ulcers.

itens.texto: It is not toxic and is produced without other polymers mixed in.
The nanofiber network handles well and molds to the skin.
It protects the wound against microbes and helps relieve pain.
It traps substances between the fibers and releases them gradually.

secoes.lede: The study was done in the lab, at the University of Sorocaba.

itens.texto: The bacterium Gluconacetobacter xylinus grew for 4 days at 30 °C in 24-well plates, forming membranes about 2 mm thick and 22 mm wide.
Jucá stem bark was collected in Rio Grande do Norte and registered at the UFRN Herbarium (no. 12181). It dried for 72 hours at 40 °C.
The 230 g of ground bark went through percolation with 70% alcohol. The liquid was concentrated and freeze-dried, yielding 88 g of extract (38%).

itens.titulo: Load the extract into the membrane
itens.texto: The membranes were soaked for 24 hours in an extract solution (100 mg/mL), with gentle shaking.
The membranes were placed in saline, and the amount of extract released was measured (by protein content) after 2, 4, 6, 24, 30 and 40 hours.
Two tests were used: the lowest concentration that stops growth (MIC) and agar diffusion, with the membrane in the center of plates with S. aureus, E. coli or P. aeruginosa.

secoes.titulo: The membrane released jucá and blocked the bacteria
secoes.lede: See the size of the protected area and the extract's strength against each bacterium.

parametros.leitura: The jucá membrane created a bacteria-free zone of about 36 mm against S. aureus (Gram-positive) and 29 mm, on average, against the Gram-negatives.
Here, the shorter the bar, the stronger the extract: little extract was enough to block E. coli. Even P. aeruginosa, which needed more, was inhibited.

blocos.nota: Halo = bacteria-free area around the membrane (mean of 3 replicates). MIC = lowest extract concentration that stopped growth.

blocos.html: The control was decisive: the nanocellulose-only membrane had no action at all against the bacteria. The jucá does the work; the nanocellulose acts as a carrier, releasing the extract gradually.

All the samples released by the membrane, from 2 to 40 hours, stopped the growth of the three bacteria: on the plates, only the positive controls formed colonies. The authors suggest that the extract's proteins may be responsible for part of this effect.

secoes.lede: The idea is to add jucá's power to nanocellulose's protection and slow release.

itens: Jucá extract enters the nanofiber network
The membrane releases the extract gradually (peak at 30 hours)
The membrane also protects the wound as a barrier

blocos.html:
Nanocellulose alone does not kill bacteria. But its structure is excellent for trapping substances without strong chemical bonds, which lets the active ingredient come out easily. There may be a small loss of activity during this release.

The results match jucá's traditional use on wounds, ulcers and skin lesions. For comparison, an earlier study found an MIC of 4,000 µg/mL for jucá against the tuberculosis bacterium, much higher than the values found here.

secoes.titulo: What the study allows us to say
secoes.lede: A promising combination that still needs to be tested for healing.

blocos.html: Both the jucá extract in solution and the extract inside nanocellulose showed action against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. According to the authors, the jucá-loaded membrane brings together the best of both components and could be a new system for delivering bioactive molecules to the skin.

blocos.titulo: Next step pointed out by the authors
itens: Assess whether the jucá membrane actually helps wounds heal.

glossario.def: Brazilian tree, also called pau-ferro (Brazilian ironwood), used in folk medicine for wound healing.
Pure cellulose in the form of nanofibers, produced by bacteria. Widely used in dressings.
Liquid or powder that concentrates the substances taken from a plant.
Technique in which a liquid (here, 70% alcohol) slowly passes through the plant powder, carrying its compounds.
Drying at low temperature under vacuum, which turns the extract into powder without damaging the compounds.
Minimum inhibitory concentration: the smallest amount that stops the bacterium from growing.
Area around the material, on the plate, where bacteria did not grow.
Lab test that measures the amount of protein in a sample through a color change.
Saline solution with controlled pH, similar to body fluids.
The two large groups of bacteria, which differ in their cell wall.
Plant compounds with an astringent taste and antimicrobial and healing action.
Scientific collection of dried, cataloged plants, which ensures the species is correctly identified.
